INTERVIEW WITH
ERSKINE HAWKINS

JAZZ ORAL HISTORY PROJECT
NATIONAL ENDOWMENT FOR THE ARTS
INSTITUTE OF JAZZ STUDIES

INTERVIEWED BY:
LEONARD GOINES
FEBRUARY 6, 1982
TAPE 1, SIDE A
This is the first session, oral history interview with Erskine Hawkins, the Concord Hotel, February 6, 1982. 11 a.m.
Erskine, your full name is Erskine Ramsey Hawkins?
That's correct.
Okay. And, can you give us a little idea of what your early history was like, including the things that you remember about your family? But first of all, when were you born?
The year of 1914, July the 26th.
Okay.

Well, I was, my father was a butcher. My mother, she was just a regular housewife. And then, I have also one sister and three other brothers. Well, I started right there at Tuogle Institute in Birmingham, Alabama. That school was right across the street from where I lived. See, all I had to do was just cross the

street and go, and jump the fence and there I was on the campus. Mrs. Tuggle, who was the founder of the school, she was very close to my family then. So, I used to play tin cans and things when the band come out at the end of the session to parade and close the school for that day. Well, I was too small to go out in the street. So, when I did, my father, I'm getting a little ahead of myself. My father passed (inaudible). He died when I was about 7 years old. Mrs. Tuggle told my family, said I'm gonna take that boy and put him in school. So, she put me in school and from then on I just stayed in the band room practically, or either on the athletic field as I grew.

So, up to the age of 14 when she passed, and then I was able to play 'Taps.' And then they had me to play 'Taps' over her grave. All through that time, I played drums, alto horn, a little sax, a little baritone horn. The trumpet I picked up last.
This was in Birmingham?
In Birmingham.
All right. And, the first instrument you played then, actually was the drum set?
The drums.
And how did you happen to do that?

Well, I started just like I said. I'd take two sticks and beat on tin cans. And then, of course, we had a picket fence and I used to play that. And then, when I got to the age of maybe 6, I'm not sure, 6, just large enough to carry a snare drum, then they put me in the band. Then I just crew from there. I played drums for about 2 years. Then, I went into alto horn.
Did your father play an instrument?
No. He was a butcher. He was in the meat factory there.
So, he didn't play any instruments then?
No. I had the other
part of the family, like a first cousin, Johnny Richardson. He was a bass player. H was supposed to have been, he was rated the best bass player around that part of the country.
And so, he used to do a lot with me and teach me. And also, my first cousin, a brother, he told me, he gave me my first horn.

So, the family, my mother was in the choir in church. Practically, my whole family - my aunts, my uncles - they all sang in the choir. So, when I was, got to be about 9, and playing my horn, I used to go and start playing my horn with them in the choir.
So, your mother sang as did other members of your family.
Right.
But, did she play an instrument?
No, she didn't.
She didn't play an instrument. Okay. Did you have any brothers or sisters?
One sister and three brothers. My brother, next to me, he played

trumpet. But, he didn't go out for it like I did. And my other two brothers, they just played around with drums. They'd never get right into it. But, they passed after they came out of the war, second World War. They had, during the war, they kinda got it there.
So, and then after the drums, you played the trombone was it? Or, the trumpet?
Alto horn.
Alto horn.

Right. Alto horn, I don't remember how (inaudible) because I had, in the band room, I just used to go and pick this instrument up and pick this instrument up, you know, until I learned to play a little something on them.

So, that's how I happened to pick those instruments up. And, I used to play them all. When we, the band go out for parades, the band master used to bring the band back and line them up in front of my house. And, he had me come out to play my solo. And, I must have been,
I was still younger than 10. And so, the whole family would just walk out on the front porch to see what happened.
Do you remember at that point that you actually started playing trumpet?
At that point, no. I didn't pay too much attention to trumpet. I could pick it up and play scales on it.
Right.
My teacher at that time, he was a trumpet player.
And who was he?

S.B. Foster. We used to call him 'High C' Foster. Yeah. And, going out on parade one day, when he came back after the parade, he took me and put me on trumpet. Before that, he used to come over my house like 5:00 in the morning and knock on the window. My mother would wake me up and say Professor Foster's out there waiting for you.
So, he used to carry me over to the school while he practices before he played the
bucle for the students to get up. See, it was, the school was a boarding school. See?
Right.
So, he used to, I was so small, he used to sit me up there on a shelf so I could hear him practicing. So, that's, I guess that's how I got interested in trumpet - just listening at him play.
So, at one time, he got short of trumpets. And, he just took me off another instrument and put me on trumpet. And then, I just went from there.
Okay. And about how old were you at this time that you began playing trumpet?
Well, I don't know. I think at about 14.
About 14.
Right.
And what was the name of your school?
Tuggle Institute.
Tuggle Institute.
Right.
And you were there for how many years?
I was there until my eleventh grade, my twelfth grade.
About twelfth grade.
Right.
And you started there at.....?
I started at kindergarten.
Started at kindergarten and went straight through until the twelfth grade.
Right.

And, how did you sort of settle on the trumpet? Because, evidently, that became the most important of the instruments that you were dealing with. How did that fit to you? How did that one sort of take over in terms of the drums and all of the others that you were playing around with?
Well, that's getting

into the big band thing. Of course, while I was playing trumpet there, I used to sit down in the school band. And when I got tired of playing trumpet, I'd sit in the saxophone section just to keep up and play the saxophone.

Well, when I got to New York and I was still playing all those instruments, I used to go into a theater like the Apollo, and Savoy Bar Room, and when different guest bands came in the Savoy Bar Room, whoever the band leader was, if he was playing trombone or saxophone or drums, I used to have a tune that I used to play and go around the band and play different instruments. And when I got to the instrument the leader was playing, just having fun you know, with the leader because we was all good friends, I'd play an instrument that he was playing. And when we did come off, we'd have a nice conversation.

That was during the time of Dorsey, Basie, well, all the big bands, Bunny Berigan, Krupa. When Krupa was there, I marched out and sat down on the drums by him. Now, you know, I had some nerve. You know. (Laughter) (Inaudible).
So, Mr. Foster was actually your first teacher?
Yes. I had, I had a teacher before that used to, I used to fake. You go, like you fake?
Right.

In other words, if I hear a tune on the radio before I learned to read, I could listen at that tune on the radio and go and pick up any instrument and play that tune without knowing how to read. So, when I got to a certain point, they said, they said well, we gonna learn you how to read. I must have been about, I guess I must have been about 7 or 8 years old. So, they took a big blackboard and put it in front of me and they made some notes, put a clef there, and then on. So, that's when I started to learn to read. Then, Professor Foster came in after that.
Right.
The teacher before
Robinson?
Right.
The first name?
The first name I can't I can't get to.
Was it Mr. or Mrs.?
Mr.
Mr.
Mr. Robinson.
Robinson.
Yeah. He was a clarinet player.
And mostly, you studied notation and theory and things like that, or did you study an instrument with him?
Well, I studied, well, I was playing drums under him.
Right.
Drums and alto. I studied just a little instrument under him. But, Robinson came in very soon after that.
Okay.
I mean, Foster came in very soon after that.
Right. Was it Mr. Robinson or Mr. Foster that taught you to read first?
Robinson started. He started me to read.
He started you. Okay.
And then, Foster picked me right up.
Right. And you were around 7 at that time.
7 or 8 years old.
And you stayed with Professor Foster from then on until?
I went to 'Bama State.
Until you went to 'Bama State.
Right.
So actually, much of your background training and everything from beginning up to your professional level was done with Professor Foster?
Right. That's correct.
So, can you tell me something about Professor Foster?

Well, he was an amazing man. He, at the time before I met him, he had been playing with the carnival. They called him "High C" Foster. And when I met him, he used to sit up there and hit a C above high C, altissimo high C.
Right.

And once while we were just parading, he let all the trumpet players out. Now, we've got a 50 piece band. And, he got mad with them for something. So, he did that whole parade by himself, playing trumpet with, what, about 5 trombones, a regular field band. And, I'll never forget that.
And then, we had to get him about 5 sticks of gum and chew that gum. He was some, he was some fellow.
Do you have any idea of what kind of training Professor Foster had?

No, I don't. I really don't. I don't know just what training he had because I understand that before that he was at the school before I was old enough to go to school. Then he went away. Then, he came back. Professor Watley, well, maybe you heard of him. J.T. Watley in Birmingham?
Yes. Sure.

Well, Professor Foster, I understand, taught Professor Watley. Professor Watley used to do a lot of things with me on account of Foster teaching me, although he was at another school right there in Birmingham, the Industrial High School. So, that's how I had my little in, and Professor J.T. Watley was very close with my family. My grandfather and uncles were carpenters. So, they built Professor Watley's house. And, they also built the school. And I didn't know, this was before I was born. And also, after the school first burned down for awhile, they rebuilt it. It was a big school, though. They thought I was gonna be a
carpenter. Well, if they put me between them, flooring and everything, I could do a little of that at that age. They went and I went the other way.
By the way, I got my scholarship at [Chuckles] 'Bama State playing tennis. I went to a relay at Tuskegee for Tuggle Institute. That was tennis. I went crazy about tennis.

Basketball. I was the captain of my basketball team. All this. If they couldn't find me in the band room, they'd find me on the athletic field. Those two spots they could always find me. They didn't have to look for me.
So, I went out there. I eliminated Talladega in tennis, and 'Bama State in tennis. So, that's how I happened to get my scholarship to go to 'Bama State.
Then, they organized another band there and they found out about my music. They actually didn't know about music. Then, they asked me to leave that alone and go stay in the band.
Okay. So, that gives

us a pretty good idea of the kind of training that you had before you went to 'Bama State. But, what kind of opportunities for music making had you had from the time that you began playing around 7, up until the time that you went to 'Bama State?
Well, there (inaudible) used to be a band leader there. I can't recall his name right now. It may come to me later. He used to play out the "Tuxedo Junction". George Uge was the name.
George?

George Uge. He was a drummer. He used to come to my house and pick me up. My mother would let me go. And, we used to, I used to play certain parties and dances for him. During the summertime, I was out to Tuxedo Junction. I played a whole summer while school was at recess. And then, I got a lot of opportunities to do those things with those musicians. I didn't get too much other training, you know. Just myself.
Right. And, how old were you when you were doing this kind of jobbing?

I was doing that between, I was, it was, oh. I started doing that when I was about 10, 12. Then, I was doing the school time. And then, in the summertime, I went up to this, I was 16 years old. And then, from that part, George Uge played there all the summer.
And, that's where I did a lot of playing and got a lot of education from that, from the jazz field.
And what kind of playing did you do in school?
Just the military, just the school music.
Just the school music.
Marching music, military music. I did a little, they had a small symphony band. In 'Bama State they had a sumphony band. And, I went in there because I did, played french horn in that. They couldn't
find no one to play french horn. So, I took it for a month to practice. Then, I sat down and played the french horn.
Yeah. I'd like to go back for a minute to something you were saying before.
You mentioned that your family members, including yourself, were all singing in a church. Which church was that?
Enon Ridge Church there in Birmingham. That's, it was not too far from my home.

My grandfather, that's, he was in what they call like an amen corner. And my uncles and my aunts, they was in the church. And then I used to, after I got old enough, at least so I could have my horn, I could, I went down and I joined them.
Right. And, what are some of your memories of the church?
Oh, it was all good memories because I went, I did quite a bit in church. But, I haven't had a chance to keep it

up now. But, I started like Sunday school, Bible classes, and things. I stayed right there because my family was deep in religion. You know, they was, they liked that. So, I had to go there. I had to make everything.
When you say deep in religion, what do you mean?

Well, I couldn't play my horn in the house. They believed, you know. I had to wait till I get into school, especially as long as my grandfather was living. You know, he was, he was very, he felt maybe the trumpet wasn't supposed to be played then. But, when I went to church with my horn, the rest of the people started to enjoy it and go out for it, especially the pastor. Then, he went with it, too. And then, from then on, he was, he was really wonderful to me.
And, when did you begin playing in church?
About, when I was about 9 years old.
When you were about 9
Just the regular hymns, whatever they were singing. You know, church hymns.
Right. And, did you play those with other people, or were you playing by yourself?
No. I was playing with the choir. Every now and then, they'd let me have a few bars as long as I didn't jazz it up.
Okay. Did you sing in that choir, too?
No. I didn't do any singing. I just played.
Yeah. And, what kind of music was it? Gospel music primarily? Or, what kind of church was it, come to think of it?
Methodist.
Methodist church.
It was Gospel tunes, you know. Not sanctified because you'd get too happy.
Get too happy.
You know, that's too happy. It's was medium.
And, what about your brothers and sisters? I mean, what did....?

My sister is still at home. She has a home there now. Like I said, my brothers, they passed on. You know, not too far behind each other because they, after going into the service, when they came back, they weren't quite together. Whatever happened, they were one was in the European, one was in the Pacific.

And, one of my brothers, when he, my youngest brother, when he came back, I brought him to New York with me to stay with me, to stick with me and with my big band. He just went in with me to do and help me out around the band, you know, because, until he kind of got himself together. Then, he went back home.
Right.
But, that was Joe, and James, and Edward.

James played trumpet while he was in the service. And my sister now, she's still at home. I was talking to her the other day, with her family. She has two kids now - Frederick and Walweesa. I can't understand just why she gave her that name. But, that's the name she did - Walweesa Erskellina Weaver. That's beautiful after I got used to it.
Right.
But, you know, she wanted part of my name with it, which was her first child. So, she called, made the middle name Erskellina.
So, she and I were the only ones left in the main family now besides some cousins.

What was Birmingham like when you think back over all of those years at the time that you were in school and playing in the church? What about the social environment? What was it like? What do you remember?
Well, I didn't know too much about that because, on account of my age. I didn't, I was there on the campus, and
across the street from there is my home. But, and then when George Uge used to come and pick me up to take me out to play different parties, that's about all I got around to beside Tuxedo Park.
So, but, it was, it was, it wasn't bad. It was nice as far as I can see about it.
Right.

Like now, it's beautiful down there now. You know. I go down there every year. I was down doing concerts. They put a plaque out to Tuxedo Junction with my name on it cause that's where I named Tuxedo Junction from Birmingham. I guess you know about that.
Yes.
Yeah. But, during that time, I didn't get around too much there. I used to stay right there near the school and my home.
But, for the purposes of the interview, why don't you tell us something about Tuxedo Park and Tuxedo Junction and all of that.

Well, Tuxedo Junction, like I said before, was where we used to get off the streetcar, which is Tuxedo Junction. From there, I used to walk a couple of blocks to Tuxedo Park. Now, this is something where they had all kinds of entertainment. It's, well, like the ferris wheel, swimming pool. You know, everything that you have to get around to. It's like a regular park I should say.

So, it was a lot of fun. So, we started playing out there in the afternoon and I think we quit about 7:00 at night, 8:00 cause there wasn't nothing out there at night. Then, we'd go back to Tuxedo Junction which is a couple of blocks to get on the streetcar. And, we'd ride back to the city. You know, it's a suburb right in the city, which was the subway to Birmingham.
Well, let me see, like Willie Mays, a few others, you know, all of them stayed out there. I'm trying to figure out who else I could call. I didn't know them, though, when I was at Tuxedo.
The way it is right now, you wouldn't know it. All they have there now is the big plaque at the building. But, everything is changed like other cities. But, it's beautiful, though.

You mentioned that Willie Mays, now that you look back at when it was there at the time, and I began to wonder. Were you in contact with any of the musicians that you were going to play with later or that you were going to meet later? Did you grow up with any of them? Or, were any of them in school with you?
Yeah. Bob, the late Bob Range. He was at Tuggle with me. He was a trombone player with me. And Edward Sims Sales. He was a trombone player with me.
Dud Bascomb. He went to Industrial High. He stayed about 2 blocks from me in Birmingham. He used to have to pass my house on his way with his horn in his hand, going to Industrial High.
When I got to 'Bama State, well,

then, that's, well, I met Haywood Henry, Sammy Lowe; Julian Dash I met in New York. He went to 'Bama State the year after we left; Big Jack Marshall, who was drums; Jimmy Mitchelle; I'm trying to think of, Marcellus Marsalis Green - but he's passed on. Like most, a lot of the boys are gone. Well, then there, let me see, Paul Bascomb which was Dud Bascomb's brother. He joined me in New York. I said Julian joined me in New York, too, because he went to 'Bama State the year after I left. Well, that's, J.B. Sims.

At the time I was sitting down in the band playing, knocking the numbers off and calling the tunes, I had him in front, directing. He was there. Well, I had contact with a lot of them when I got to 'Bama State.
Right. But, before you got to 'Bama State, you didn't have contact with most of them?
Not with most of them. But, it's like, I knew Sammy Lowe's brother, J. L. Lowe. He used to come out and try to keep me up on my studies at 'Bama State. He was a

saxophone player and everything.
So, I met Sammy Lowe later on
because Dud Bascomb knew Sam cause they went to
school together at Industrial High.

So, I got ready to get in front of
to send for Sam
the band and Dud made the suggestion (inaudible).
You know, so for trumpet.
Right.

That's how it happened that Sam did a lot of arrangements for me
in the band.

Okay. Were there any
other things that you can think of that either
you remember that were significant in terms of
your development as a person, or that you can
think of in terms of having some kind of influence on you musically? This is before you
went to 'Bama State. I mean, any other thing
that we haven't touched on yet.

Well, the main thing,
I wouldn't say the man thing, was it seemed like
I just had it in me at that time according to
people. But, I wanted that and it was on

account of my cousins playing their instruments to get into it, which was Johnny Richardson, and my first cousin's brother, my first cousin's husband's brother. He gave me the trumpet. And they, I just stuck around with them most of the time wherever they would go on account of it. And then from there, I went to the school. That's what gave me the thrust to stick with the music. And so, I could sit up there and pick up that horn and play, pick up any instrument and play most anything I'd hear before I could read. And then, other bands. I started listening to bands like Duke. They used to come to Birmingham for, to play one night stands. I used to sit up and climb the window to try and get in there. I was too young to go in and catch the band. And, they influenced me a lot. That's, here was one big band that I wanted to be in. I had Louis Armstrong. After I heard him coming out of New Orleans, I used to buy all his records, everyone I could get my hands on. When I started playing it, I'd try to copy every solo that he played, and things like "Shine", and

"I'm Confessing That I Love You". I used to do that, that "Shine". I used to do that and try to, and do it like a hundred, high C like Louis used to do a certain amount and the boys used to count come up behind him.
Right.

And, they used, down there, they used to call me "Iron Lung" on account I could last so long. And Louis, Louis really gave me the influence thrust by him being a trumpet, and after I picked it up that I wanted to stick with it.
You know, then I finally met Louis after I got to New York. He came up and did a number with me. That made me, I was sure I guess I'd just better stay here.

What kind of places did you have to hear music because you mentioned that you were too young to actually go in to hear some of these players, but you wanted to hear them. What kind of places did you have, or opportunities did you have to hear live musicians?

Well, in Birmingham and at the school, at the school a lot of bands come through with Earl Hines during those years. And, Earl Hines came back to New York. He'd tell Joe Glaser all about that. And, that's the only place that I actually did hear was in Birmingham. That was at the Elks Place. That's where they said I was too young to get in. So. I used to stand outside and try to look through the windows cause I couldn't get in. And, all the other times, I couldn't, this was just like radio.
I didn't go nowhere. I didn't go out. (Inaudible). That's kind of close.
Right.

That's pretty close through my life. I got most of mine through the radio. Every night, when I was in school, I used to sit up there and have that radio on when it's late at night under the pillow, to listen.
And what kinds of things were on the radio at that time that you remember?

Well, I had the big bands that was broadcasting. You know, that was a big time it seems. That was a big time of year that, oh, I'm trying to think of some of the names of some of the bands that used to broadcast. Clyde McCoy, I used to get him a lot. I even had, well, that's doing it, Isham Jones. You know, besides the Duke, and Earl Hines and Louis. Those seem to be some of the main bands that I got at that time, whenever I could.
And then, after I got to 'Bama State, I went to New Orleans. And, that's where I got a lot of things.
You mentioned before that Earl Hines had told Joe Glaser something about you?

Right. I, oh yeah. I was in 'Bama State then. Earl Hines came down with his band to play a concert on the campus and I was in school then. And, we each would alternate. We did that with all the bands that came there.
So, when Earl got back to Chicago,

Earl told Joe Glaser about me. That, of course, is just like I said. I just, high notes than (inaudible) to me were nothing. I mean, cause I was used to it. You know? I was hitting the C on account of, well, Foster. I used to try and copy everything he did, go through like he would hit that al-tissimo high C then. And then, I just started to try and keep up with him. You know?
Right.

And then, I told Joe Glaser about him a month later. Joe sent a letter and a ticket, and also, oh, let me see, about $100 for a little money. But, I kept that month, and I thought it over (inaudible). My aunt told me, she was living in New Jersey, in Newark. I told her I was going to Chicago. I had an opportunity to go to Chicago. So, thought it out. She said you'd better stay there cause she was, and if you're going away, you'd better come to New York. So, in case things don't work out for you, I can kinda help look out for you. So, I got back in touch with Joe Glaser, thanked him very much, and Joe told me,
said if anytime you want me or need me in New York or anywhere, just let me know. It was very nice of him. He and I were still friends up until the time he passed.
And so, I went to New York with the band. Then, I got a break at the Harlem Opera House.
Sure. Absolutely.

So, we went in there, and had never played a stage show before. We had Jackie "Moms" Mabley, the Steppe Brothers. We don't know nothing about show music, but we, they taught us. And, Christina Banks and the chorus line.
I'd like to stay before 'Bama State, you know, for a little while. We're gonna get right to that a little later.
All right.

I wanted to ask you because you had mentioned how easy it was for you to just pick up, you know, all of these various instruments and to work with it. But, to develop this fantastic range and endurance
and all of that that you have on trumpet. I mean, that's not very easy. I mean, it isn't even possible for everybody to do that. Now, how did you go about that?

Well, I heard Steve, [Tommy Stevenson] Ben Stevens. I think he was playing trumpet with Jimmy Lunceford. And, I tried it with the mouthpiece that I had. You know, a regular mouthpiece, and I couldn't make it.

So, right then, it seemed like it was too small. I couldn't find one that was cut large enough for me. So, I took an old mouthpiece, took a file, sandpaper, put it on the paper, shaved it down, took the file and filed it down, cut it out, made that, made it a little wider, a little shallower inside. And, I kept on doing it until I got it the way my mouth felt comfortable. And then, I took it to a place and let them smooth it down, then played it.
And, I got used to that mouthpiece. And then I, my chops, they're a little thick. But, the mouthpiece I had was a little too small

for me. So, I started hitting notes and kept on practicing and kept on till I got it like I wanted. So, I kept using my own mouthpiece. I still got my own mouthpiece. After that, LaVelle after that made some for me.
So, I started hitting notes at that time after I shaved my own mouthpiece, and kept my own mouthpiece.
What kinds of things did you practice?
Oh, I stayed in the book a lot, and then I practiced things on my own - scales, going from one staff to another staff, and the scales, chords and everything.

Give me an idea of what your normal, keeping in shape routine would be like. I mean, how you would, the things you would practice, and the amount of time and whatever. Say, just take a normal week while you were in school at that time.
Well, after class, before the band rehearsal, I used to go in the band room and just pick up my instrument and

start to blow scales or anything, and just kept trying for certain things that I hadn't tried to play before, even going higher and higher. I did that like during lunchtime, when the school was out which was 3:00 I believe. I stayed there in that band room until like 6:00 in the evening still playing, still practicing and doing everything that I couldn't do because I knew when I would go home, I couldn't practice it there.

So, I did that say every day in the week. I never did miss a day in the week by not practicing. You know, Sunday was the only time I wasn't in school, and when I got old enough, I was doing that in church.

Then, Professor Foster, he used to have certain things for me to practice, a certain book. So, he believed in that because he'd pick me up like 4, 5:00 in the morning and carry me over there to the band room. That's even before the students got up. And, I'd sit up there and practice along with him at times. And, he showed me a lot. And, I'm his best, that was the man.
What size a band did you have in school there when you were going?
You're talking about the school band?
Yes, the school band.
It wasn't too large. It was something like 35. And, I think the largest we went to was about 50 pieces. The school band.
Did you play piano at all during this time?
